paragraphs.text: A loose [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from Guangxi, made in the 1990s, that has been abroad and come home. The shop traces it from Guangzhou to storage in Malaysia and Singapore, then back to Guangzhou. That round trip is what [returned](malaysian-returned-liu-bao:returned) means, huiliu in Chinese: the Malaysia in its name marks a stop in the life of the tea, not the place the leaf was grown.

It travelled an old road. Liu Bao was made for Chinese miners and labourers in Malaya, above all in the [tin mines](liu-bao:nanyang-trade), where the trade believed it eased the heat and damp of the work. A trade account published in 1951 follows the tea downriver, onto a larger wooden boat at Libu for Fengkai and then a powered vessel for Guangzhou, with [Ipoh and Kuala Lumpur](malaysian-returned-liu-bao:river-trade) among its final markets. Older tea from that trade later found buyers back in China.

At thirty-one years it is far past the ten the trade needs to count a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged), and its years overseas are part of that age: where a Liu Bao was stored matters as much as how long.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
